title: Chapter 23 — The Lee Shore
paragraphs: Some chapters back, a man named Bulkington was mentioned — a tall, recently landed sailor encountered at the inn in New Bedford.

When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bow into the cold, hostile waves, who should I see standing at the helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in the dead of winter, having just returned from a four-year dangerous voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy stint at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken. Deep memories yield no epitaphs. This six-inch chapter is the gravestone — without a stone — of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with a storm-tossed ship driven helplessly along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter. The port is compassionate. In the port there is safety, comfort, a warm hearth, supper, blankets, friends — everything kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is the ship's greatest danger. She must refuse all hospitality. One touch of land, even grazing the keel, would make her shudder from stem to stern. With all her might she crowds on sail to get offshore. In doing so, she fights the very winds that would blow her home. She seeks the open, landless sea again — rushing into danger for the sake of refuge. Her only friend is her bitterest enemy!

Do you understand now, Bulkington? Do you catch a glimpse of that unbearable truth — that all deep, earnest thinking is nothing but the brave effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea, while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, enslaving shore?

But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and infinite as God — it is better to die in that howling infinity than to be shamefully smashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who, worm-like, would crawl cringing to land! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Stand firm, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up leaps your immortality!
